original.text: Devahitabrāhmaṇavatthu Pubbenivāsaṁ yo vedi, saggāpāyañca passati; Atho jātikkhayaṁ patto, abhiññāvosito muni; Sabbavositavosānaṁ, tamahaṁ brūmi brāhmaṇaṁ. Brāhmaṇavaggo chabbīsatimo. Ettāvatā sabbapaṭhame yamakavagge cuddasa vatthūni, appamādavagge nava, cittavagge nava, pupphavagge dvādasa, bālavagge pannarasa, paṇḍitavagge ekādasa, arahantavagge dasa, sahassavagge cuddasa, pāpavagge dvādasa, daṇḍavagge ekādasa, jarāvagge nava, attavagge dasa, lokavagge ekādasa, buddhavagge nava, sukhavagge aṭṭha, piyavagge nava, kodhavagge aṭṭha, malavagge dvādasa, dhammaṭṭhavagge dasa, maggavagge dvādasa, pakiṇṇakavagge nava, nirayavagge nava, nāgavagge aṭṭha, taṇhāvagge dvādasa, bhikkhuvagge dvādasa, brāhmaṇavagge cattālīsāti pañcādhikāni tīṇi vatthusatāni. Satevīsacatussatā, catusaccavibhāvinā; Satattayañca vatthūnaṁ, pañcādhikaṁ samuṭṭhitāti. Dhammapade vaggānamuddānaṁ Yamakappamādo cittaṁ, pupphaṁ bālena paṇḍito; Arahanto sahassañca, pāpaṁ daṇḍena te dasa. Jarā attā ca loko ca, buddho sukhaṁ piyena ca; Kodho malañca dhammaṭṭho, maggavaggena vīsati. Pakiṇṇaṁ nirayo nāgo, taṇhā bhikkhu ca brāhmaṇo; Ete chabbīsati vaggā, desitādiccabandhunā. Gāthānamuddānaṁ Yamake vīsati gāthā, appamādamhi dvādasa; Ekādasa cittavagge, pupphavaggamhi soḷasa. Bāle ca soḷasa gāthā, paṇḍitamhi catuddasa; Arahante dasa gāthā, sahasse honti soḷasa. Terasa pāpavaggamhi, daṇḍamhi dasa satta ca; Ekādasa jarā vagge, attavaggamhi tā dasa. Dvādasa lokavaggamhi, buddhavaggamhi ṭhārasa; Sukhe ca piyavagge ca, gāthāyo honti dvādasa. Cuddasa kodhavaggamhi, malavaggekavīsati; Sattarasa ca dhammaṭṭhe, maggavagge sattarasa. Pakiṇṇe soḷasa gāthā, niraye nāge ca cuddasa; Chabbīsa taṇhāvaggamhi, tevīsa bhikkhuvaggikā. Ekatālīsagāthāyo, brāhmaṇe vaggamuttame; Gāthāsatāni cattāri, tevīsa ca punāpare; Dhammapade nipātamhi, desitādiccabandhunāti. Dhammapadapāḷi samattā.

paraphrase: Chapter 16, Piyavagga, verses 209-220. paraphrase: The Dhammapada gathers 423 verses in 26 vaggas on a single course: mind (mano) is the forerunner and chief of things (dhammā), and suffering or happiness follows what one says and does with a corrupt or a clear mind (1-2); the mind (citta) is unsteady and needs guarding and taming (33-43), and through heedfulness (21-32), restraint of body, speech and mind (231-234), the abandonment of craving (334-359), and seeing with wisdom that all formations are impermanent and suffering and all dhammas not-self (277-279), one comes to nibbāna, the supreme happiness (203-204) and to the freedom described in the arahant and the 'brāhmaṇa' (90-99, 383-423). By the six marks of purport: (1) opening and closing: the text opens with mind as forerunner (1-2) and closes with the description of the one freed, called a brāhmaṇa by conduct rather than birth (383-423); (2) repetition: the paired and serial verses (1-20, 100-102, 110-115, 212-216, 296-301, 356-359, and the refrain 'him I call a brāhmaṇa' in most verses of 385-423), and the repeated 'oneself' verses (157-166, 379-380); (3) novelty: titles such as brāhmaṇa, samaṇa, bhikkhu, muni, thera and ariya are redefined by conduct (142, 261, 264-270, 388, 393-396); (4) stated results: happiness follows a clear mind (2), nibbāna is near (32, 372), the taints end (226, 293), the freed do not grieve (225, 336, 412); (5) praise (arthavāda): heedfulness praised (21-32), one word of Dhamma over a thousand (100-102), the fruit of stream-entry over sovereignty of the earth (178), the gift of Dhamma over all gifts (354); (6) reasoned demonstration by images: the well and badly roofed house (13-14), the fletcher and the arrow (33, 80), drops filling a jar (121-122), the cut tree that grows again (338), the wheel following the ox (1), the shadow that never leaves (2). The verses are addressed variously and often unnamed; the frame stories belong to the commentary and are not used here.
